Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

The world is a dangerous place
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'permanently humiliated' is hard to reconcile unless the illness involved a specifically shaming interpersonal circumstance; nothing else in the profile suggests that context. The other items center danger, fear, vivid reliving, and generalized threat, so humiliation stands out as clinically mismatched to the trauma type.

vignette:
Arthur, at 78, still kept a meticulous schedule as a database administrator, a profession that demanded precision and calm. Yet, calm was a luxury he rarely experienced anymore. It had been nearly two years since the sudden, brutal onset of sepsis had plunged him into an intensive care unit, fighting for his life against an infection that ravaged his system. He remembered the sterile, metallic tang of the oxygen mask, the faint, cloying sweetness of the intravenous medications, and the pervasive, almost industrial scent of disinfectant that seemed to cling to everything. Those smells, he found, were now etched into his very being. Sometimes, when he was simply reading a report or even just making a cup of tea in his kitchen, the faint whiff of a cleaning product or a particular hospital-like aroma would suddenly transport him back. The memory wouldn't just be a thought; it would feel like the frantic beeping of monitors was echoing in his ears, the coldness of the sheets against his skin, the urgent voices of the nurses. It felt real, more vivid and immediate than any ordinary memory, as if he were back in that bed, gasping for breath, the fear a cold knot in his stomach.

That harrowing experience had fundamentally shifted Arthur's perception of the world. He had come to believe, with a chilling certainty, that the world was a profoundly dangerous place, full of unseen threats. His faith, once a quiet comfort, had been shattered; how could a benevolent power allow such suffering, or how could life be anything but fragile and unpredictable? What frightened him most, however, was the insidious betrayal of his own body. Even now, long after his physical recovery, the slightest ache, a momentary shortness of breath, or an unusual sensation would send a jolt of panic through him. He was certain his body was an enemy, constantly threatening to turn against him again, reacting as if the danger was still present, even when he was objectively safe and well.

This pervasive sense of threat had infiltrated every corner of Arthur's life. At home, in his quiet apartment filled with books and the hum of his computer, he felt perpetually on guard. Every creak of the floorboards, every distant siren, made him jump, his senses heightened, constantly scanning for signs of danger, an unseen threat. He was hyperalert, watching, listening, unable to truly relax. This constant vigilance was exhausting, leaving him with an underlying current of fear and anger that gnawed at him. He found himself lashing out at minor frustrations, experiencing bursts of irritation he couldn't control.

His work, once a source of stable routine, had become another arena for his struggles. The quiet, focused environment of his office, usually a sanctuary, sometimes made his hypervigilance worse. He'd find himself distracted by the soft whir of the servers, convinced he heard something amiss, or checking his own pulse, convinced his heart was beating too fast. He'd meticulously back up databases, not just as good practice, but driven by a deep-seated fear of catastrophic failure, a mirror of his own body's collapse. The effort required to maintain his composure and focus was immense, leading to a profound fatigue by the end of each day. He had started declining social invitations, even from his colleagues, finding the effort of pretending to be "normal" too draining, preferring the solitary safety of his guarded home.

Arthur had lived with this relentless internal siege for too long. The constant fear, the vivid, unwelcome memories, and the crushing belief that his own body and the world were against him had become unbearable. He finally sought help, not out of hope for a complete return to his old self, but out of a desperate need for a reprieve, a moment of peace from the hyperalertness that had become his unwanted constant companion. He simply wanted to feel safe again, even for a little while, in his own home, in his own skin.
